From assessment to tax bill

Every parcel is assessed once a year as of July 1 at sixty percent of its true and actual value. A county levy rate applies the following calendar year, and the county sheriff then mails the bill and collects it in halves. W. Va. Code 11-3-1 sets the assessment date as July 1 of the year before the tax year, with the tax year being the next calendar year that begins after that date.

For a seller the calendar is the useful part. The July 1 value drives next year's bill, the bill goes out in summer, and the first half is due early in September. If you close partway through the cycle, seller and buyer have to split the bill between them.

  • Assessor: sets values for real and personal property and keeps the records.
  • County commission: acts as the board of equalization and review every February.
  • Levying bodies: the state, county commission, school board and any municipality set rates, within limits.
  • Sheriff: sends the tax ticket and collects payment.

True and actual value

That phrase means the price the property would bring if the owner offered it voluntarily on the usual terms, not a forced-sale price (W. Va. Code 11-3-1(a)). For owner-occupied homes, the assessor also weighs the fair and reasonable income the property might earn as a rental under normal local conditions.

Assessors keep values current by sending a staff member to each parcel of real property in repeating three-year cycles to check for changes. The sixty percent rule is firm: assessed value must be 60 percent of true and actual value, and the tax is the levy rate applied to the assessed figure.

Property classes and maximum rates

Four property classes exist here, and each caps the rate differently.

  • Class I: tangible personal property used exclusively in agriculture, farm products held by the producer, and intangible personal property.
  • Class II: owner-occupied homes used only as residences, plus farms occupied and cultivated by their owners or bona fide tenants.
  • Class III: every other kind of real and personal property outside city limits.
  • Class IV: every other kind of real and personal property inside city limits.
Taxing authorityClass IClass IIClass IIIClass IV
State0.25 cents0.50 cents1.00 cent1.00 cent
County14.3028.6057.2057.20
Schools22.9545.9091.8091.80
Municipal12.5025.00not applicable50.00
Total maximum50.00100.00150.00200.00

The numbers are ceilings on regular levies in cents per $100 of assessed value. A county, school district or city can win voter approval for excess levies above them; the state can't go over its own rate. Statewide, the average rate across all property is $1.90 per $100 of assessed valuation. Your own rate depends on your levy district and any excess levies, so read the sheriff's ticket for the real number.

Due dates, discounts and interest

You pay in two halves (W. Va. Code 11A-1-3(a)). The first half is payable September 1 of the tax year, late after October 1. The second is payable March 1, late after April 1.

  • Assessment date: the July 1 before the tax year begins.
  • Tax tickets from sheriffs: on or after July 15 of the tax year.
  • Public utility bills from the State Auditor: June of the tax year.
  • Discount for paying by the due date: 2.5 percent.
  • Interest on delinquent taxes: 9 percent per year.

Paying by the payable date earns a discount of 2.5 percent, while the late rate is nine percent a year. Interest starts on the delinquency date and runs until you pay. Each ticket goes to the last known address by first-class mail, yet section 11A-1-8 preserves the right to collect the tax, interest or penalty even if the sheriff fails to send the ticket or the taxpayer fails to get it. After buying or selling a house, make sure the ticket is going to the right address.

Homestead exemption

It exists for older and disabled owners. W. Va. Code 11-6B-3 takes the first $20,000 of assessed value off a homestead the owner lives in, if that owner is 65 or older or certified permanently and totally disabled.

  • Two straight calendar years of West Virginia residence before the tax year are required, with narrow exceptions for people who left and came back and for certain military service members.
  • Collecting a comparable exemption in another state disqualifies you, and the application includes a sworn affidavit on the point.
  • One exemption per homestead, however many eligible owners share it.
  • The exemption attaches to the homestead occupied on the July 1 assessment date and applies to the next tax year.

A sale changes things. When a qualified owner's homestead passes by deed, will or otherwise, the new owner loses the $20,000 at the next July 1 assessment unless they qualify, so a buyer shouldn't count on the seller's lower bill. Under section 11-6B-4, an owner 65 or older who has filed once with the assessor needn't refile unless moving to a new homestead.

How to appeal your assessment

Raise it with the assessor first. If that fails, the county commission hears it in February while sitting as the board of equalization and review. Section 11-3-24 requires the commission to convene by February 1 of the tax year, lets it adjourn after February 15 and requires it to adjourn by the last day of February.

The board reviews and corrects valuation but can't decide questions of classification or taxability. For a classification dispute, section 11-3-24a lets a taxpayer ask the assessor for information and protest, with a path on to the Tax Commissioner and the Office of Tax Appeals. The board can bring any assessment found above or below sixty percent back to sixty percent, and no assessment can be raised without at least five days' written notice.

Skip the board meeting and you waive the right to seek correction of the current year's list, except by appeal to the Office of Tax Appeals or as otherwise provided. A taxpayer who elects a hearing may appeal the board's order to that office. Section 11-3-23a also provides an informal review: apply for relief to the board or the Office of Tax Appeals by February 20 of the tax year with a written protest.

The deadlines are tight and a missed February meeting can cost a year, so put them on your calendar early.

Taxes and fees when you sell

Two charges ride on the deed under W. Va. Code 11-22-2: the real property transfer tax, $1.10 per $500 of value or fraction, and a $20 fee for transferring real estate for consideration. The county clerk takes both at recording. That section also treats the excise tax as a county tax that the collecting county keeps, beginning July 1, 2025.

Recording happens at the county courthouse through the clerk, while the sheriff handles property tax. At closing, the title company or closing agent should pull a current tax statement from the sheriff, check which halves are paid, and settle any unpaid ones out of your proceeds.

Owe back taxes? Ask the county sheriff for a payoff figure before you pick a buyer. We can buy a house as-is even with tax due, and we'll go through the numbers with you. The amount depends on the house and the payoff, and we promise no price.

Frequently asked questions

What is the West Virginia property tax assessment ratio?

Sixty percent. Each year property is assessed as of July 1 at sixty percent of its true and actual value (W. Va. Code 11-3-1(a)), and the levy rate applies to that assessed figure.

When is the first half of West Virginia property tax due?

The first half comes due September 1 of the tax year and is late after October 1. The second half is due March 1 and late after April 1 (W. Va. Code 11A-1-3). Paying on time earns a 2.5 percent discount.

What interest applies to late West Virginia property tax?

Nine percent a year, from the delinquency date until the tax is paid. It applies to both halves.

Who qualifies for the homestead exemption?

An owner who lives in the home and is 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled. The first $20,000 of assessed value is exempted, and two straight calendar years of state residency are required, with the exceptions in section 11-6B-3.

Can I sell a house while property tax is still owed?

Yes. The closing normally pays the balance from your proceeds. Get the sheriff's payoff figure first, and tell any buyer what is owed.

West Virginia Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a West Virginia Homestead Exemption sale

Selling a West Virginia House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in West Virginia?
We buy West Virginia houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Who qualifies

You qualify when the house is your sole residence and you are 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled. Section 11-6B-3 of the West Virginia Code exempts the first $20,000 of assessed value of a homestead you use and occupy exclusively as a home.

The West Virginia Tax Division includes it among its property tax exemptions with the same wording: owner-occupied residential property of a person 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled. There is no income test. A homestead gets a single exemption even if several qualifying owners share it.

RequirementRule
AmountFirst $20,000 of assessed value
Owner65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled
UseUsed and occupied by the owner exclusively for residential purposes
ResidencyWest Virginia resident for the two consecutive calendar years before the tax year
Other statesNo similar exemption in another state; sworn affidavit with the application
LimitOne exemption per homestead

Residency rules and exceptions

You must have lived in West Virginia, or be about to have done so, for the two consecutive calendar years before the tax year. A voter registration card or a motor vehicle registration card issued here counts as proof, along with other documents.

Two exceptions exist. Someone who left the state and returned within five years can qualify without the two straight years, provided they were a resident for two calendar years out of the ten before the tax year. And a person who was a West Virginia resident when entering active military duty, kept the state as home through service, and came back to buy a homestead after retiring or separating because of a permanent and total disability is treated as meeting the test.

An owner who receives a similar exemption on a homestead in another state is ineligible, which is why the application carries a sworn affidavit. If you split your year between West Virginia and somewhere else, read that requirement closely before filing.

Filing and the December 1 deadline

Take the claim to the assessor of the county where the home sits, on or before December 1 following the July 1 assessment date. Section 11-6B-4 sets that date. A claimant who is sick, away or otherwise disabled can file through a duly authorized agent.

The Tax Division's property tax page has a county assessors directory for all 55 counties, with office locations, phone numbers and website links. Each assessor handles the paperwork locally.

  • File in the county where the homestead is located.
  • Beat the December 1 date that follows the July 1 assessment.
  • Attach the sworn affidavit saying no similar exemption is claimed in another state.
  • For a disability claim, attach one of the documents the statute lists.

A missed date costs you. Under section 11-6B-4, someone who doesn't file by December 1 is treated as having waived the exemption for the next tax year.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your West Virginia house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Proof of disability

A disability claim needs one of eight kinds of documentation, and the list is broad. It includes a written certification from a medical or osteopathic doctor authorized to practice in West Virginia that the claimant is permanently and totally disabled, and a Social Security Administration certification that the claimant now receives permanent and total disability benefits.

The list continues with a copy of the original Social Security award letter plus a voided copy of a current benefit check, a current Medicare card with a voided benefit check, and a written VA certification of total and permanent disability. Workers' compensation papers and pneumoconiosis papers certifying total and permanent disability also count, and the eighth item is any other lawfully recognized documentation.

A disabled claimant files once, then signs a statement agreeing to tell the assessor if eligibility ends. If the claim rested on benefits, the assessor must hear within thirty days after the benefits stop.

Do you reapply every year?

No. Once a claimant 65 or older has filed, there is no need to file again unless they move to a new homestead. Section 11-6B-4 says this directly, and a disabled claimant gets a similar rule plus the notice duty described above.

One situation that might look like a move isn't treated as one. A qualified claimant who lives with a family member, or in a nursing home, personal care home, rehabilitation center or similar facility because of illness, accident or infirmity has not moved to a new homestead. Families weighing whether to sell a parent's house during a care stay should know that.

The exemption attaches to the home the owner occupies on the July 1 assessment date and applies to the next tax year's taxes. It stays with the house. Section 11-6B-3 bars moving it to another homestead before the following July 1.

When the house is sold or inherited

On a transfer by deed, will or otherwise, the $20,000 exemption comes off at the next July 1 assessment unless the new owner qualifies. A buyer under 65 and not disabled gets nothing, so the tax bill on the same house can climb after a sale.

For a seller the effects are small but real. The current year's tax ticket still follows the schedule in section 11A-1-3: first installment payable September 1 and delinquent October 1, second payable March 1 and delinquent April 1. Pay by those payable dates for a two and one-half percent discount; late amounts carry nine percent annual interest. The county sheriff sends tickets on or after July 15.

Heirs meet the same rule when a parent who held the exemption dies. An heir who keeps the house and qualifies files a new claim by December 1. Heirs who sell can forget the exemption after the deed is recorded. Our estate and inheritance tax guide covers the other costs of an inherited house.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy West Virginia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Assessment, levies and protests

Assessed value here is 60 percent of fair market value, and the exemption is subtracted from that lower figure. What you actually save depends on local levy rates, so check your tax ticket.

Property tax is levied by county boards of education, county commissions, municipalities and the State. Under the Constitution, Class II covers owner-occupied residential property used only as a home, one of four property classes. A house in that class is what the homestead exemption was written for.

To dispute an assessed value, take the protest to the county commission sitting as a board of equalization and review. It begins meeting February 1 each year, may adjourn any time after February 15 once its work is done, and must adjourn by February 28.

  • Assessment date: July 1 each year.
  • Exemption claim deadline: December 1.
  • Protest window: the county board starts meeting February 1.
  • Tickets: issued on or after July 15.

Selling instead of keeping the house

The exemption ends with ownership. If you are 65 or older, behind on repairs and unsure whether to stay, the tax saving is one number to weigh against upkeep.

We buy houses in West Virginia as-is, with no commission and no repair requests. Tell us about the property and any tax notices you've received, and we can explain what a cash closing involves. Before you list, collect your latest tax ticket, your exemption approval and any lien notices, so the title company can see what is owed. You can decline any offer at no cost.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the West Virginia homestead exemption?

The first $20,000 of a lived-in home's assessed value is exempt. Assessed value is only 60 percent of market value, so the exemption covers more than $20,000 of what the house would sell for. What you save depends on local levy rates.

What age do I need to be to claim it?

The owner has to be 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled, and live in the house as a sole residence. Your county assessor can explain how the age date applies to you.

When is the filing deadline?

December 1, following the July 1 assessment date, with the assessor of the county where the home sits. Miss it and you are treated as having waived the exemption for the next tax year.

Do I have to file every year?

No. If you are 65 or older and filed once, you need not file again unless you move to a new homestead. Disabled claimants don't refile either, but must tell the assessor if they stop qualifying, within thirty days if benefits end.

Does the exemption pass to the buyer, and can I also claim one in another state?

It doesn't pass. After a transfer, the $20,000 comes off at the next July 1 assessment unless the new owner qualifies on their own. And no: an owner receiving a similar exemption in another state is ineligible, and the application needs a sworn affidavit saying so.

West Virginia Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Selling a West Virginia House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in West Virginia?
We buy West Virginia houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

West Virginia estate tax and inherited houses

A family selling an inherited West Virginia house will rarely owe state estate tax. The state levy is triggered only by a federal estate tax bill. Section 11-11-3 of the West Virginia Code measures it by the share of the old federal state-death-tax credit that belongs to property in this state, and begins with the words "whenever a federal estate tax is payable to the United States."

Everything turns on that first clause. The IRS instructions for Form 706 say that for 2026 deaths, a federal return is needed only above $15,000,000, counting the gross estate, adjusted taxable gifts and the specific exemption. Estates well under that line owe no federal tax, which leaves the state statute with nothing to apply to.

Section 11-11-2 defines that credit and keeps it from falling below what older federal law provided. Current IRS instructions mention the "repeal of section 2011," the old credit section, and offer a state death tax deduction on the return in its place. A very large estate should ask a probate attorney or the Tax Commissioner how the two fit.

State return and deadline

If the estate owes the tax, the personal representative sends a return to the Tax Commissioner nine months after the death at the latest. Section 11-11-8 names the Charleston office and requires an executed copy of the federal return to go with it.

An estate outside the tax files nothing. Beneficiaries can still be contacted: after a notice from the Tax Commissioner, anyone holding a legal or beneficial interest must answer questions about it.

Filing pointRuleAuthority
When the state tax appliesA federal estate tax is payableW. Va. Code 11-11-3
State return deadlineNine months after deathW. Va. Code 11-11-8(d)
Where to fileTax Commissioner, CharlestonW. Va. Code 11-11-8(e)
Federal filing level, deaths in 2026More than $15,000,000 (gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and specific exemption)IRS Form 706 instructions
Federal return timingGenerally nine months after death, with a six-month extension if requested before the due dateIRS filing guidance

The IRS describes the federal timing on its estate and gift tax returns page.

The nonprobate inventory

Within 90 days of qualifying, the personal representative files a sworn list of assets that skip the will. Section 11-11-7 wants each tangible and intangible nonprobate personal asset the decedent owned or shared, valued as of the death.

Think of jointly titled accounts and similar items that neither the will nor intestacy controls. The filing goes to the county commission clerk or the fiduciary supervisor, together with the chapter 44 appraisement form.

A house is real property, so it doesn't appear on this inventory. The same personal representative who files it is usually the person signing the sale papers.

  • Use date-of-death values.
  • The clock starts when the personal representative qualifies.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your West Virginia house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Income tax when heirs sell

Federal income tax hits only the profit over basis, and an inherited house usually starts with a basis equal to its market value at death. The IRS gifts and inheritances page allows the alternate valuation date instead when the executor files Form 706 and elects it.

Sell for more and the difference is taxable. Order a date-of-death appraisal early, return or no return, since it fixes where you begin.

The IRS adds two warnings. Under a 2015 law, some recipients must match the basis to the value finally reported on an estate tax return, and one handed a Schedule A to Form 8971 by an executor may have to report it. Claiming a basis above the final estate tax value can trigger an accuracy-related penalty.

Transfer tax at the deed

The state charges $1.10 on each $500 of value, collected as the deed goes in for recording. Section 11-22-2 applies it to whoever delivers, accepts or presents the document.

A single document bears one state tax and one county tax, taken in the county of first recording. The seller-side grantor pays, unless the grantee takes the document with the tax unpaid. Trustee transfers and clerk transfers of tax-sale land put the cost on the grantee.

There is also an added county excise tax. It started in 1968 at 55 cents per $500, and counties may increase it to equal the state rate or up to $1.65 per $500 after July 1, 2017. The first tax is itself a county excise tax that stays with the collecting county. Rates vary, so phone the clerk in the recording county.

  • Subsection (a): $1.10 per $500 of value, counting any fraction of $500.
  • Subsection (b) county add-on: 55 cents per $500, which a county can raise.
  • Due at delivery, acceptance or recording.

Property tax and homestead status

The estate keeps owing property tax, billed by the county sheriff. At the West Virginia Tax Division, status on July 1 fixes ownership, use and value for the following calendar tax year, and tickets go out on or after July 15. Assessed value is 60 percent of market value under the Constitution.

Section 11A-1-3 splits payment in two. Installment one is payable September 1 and goes delinquent October 1; installment two is payable March 1 and goes delinquent April 1. A two and one-half percent discount rewards paying by the payable date, while late balances accrue nine percent annual interest from delinquency.

Inheriting can raise the bill. A decedent aged 65 or older may have had the $20,000 homestead exemption, and section 11-6B-3 strips it at the next July 1 assessment after any transfer, whether by deed, will or otherwise, unless the new owner qualifies. An heir living in the house who is 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled, may. Our homestead exemption guide covers that filing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy West Virginia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Cash sale for heirs

Heirs who sell for cash hand over the house in its current condition, skipping repairs, showings and a buyer's mortgage approval. The personal representative signs the contract and deed. A title company reviews liens and the estate's authority, and the transfer tax is paid when the deed is recorded.

  • Confirm who the qualified personal representative is before signing anything.
  • Obtain a written value as of death, because it sets the heirs' basis.
  • Bring property tax installments up to date before closing.
  • Ask the county clerk to quote the transfer tax.

You can say no to any offer at no cost, and we promise no particular price or timeline.

Frequently asked questions

Does West Virginia have an inheritance tax?

The code shows an estate tax but no separate levy on beneficiaries. Section 11-11-3 applies only if a federal estate tax is payable. A large or unusual estate should check with a probate attorney or the Tax Commissioner.

What is the federal estate tax filing level for 2026?

A Form 706 is due for 2026 deaths when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific exemption tops $15,000,000. Smaller estates owe no federal return on that ground.

When is a West Virginia estate tax return due?

Nine months after death, for an estate that owes the tax. Send it to the Tax Commissioner in Charleston with a copy of the federal return. An estate outside the tax files nothing.

Do heirs pay capital gains tax on an inherited house?

Only on profit over basis. Basis normally equals the value at death, so a prompt sale near that price usually shows little or no gain. Save your appraisal with your tax records.

What happens to the homestead exemption when an heir takes over?

It drops off at the next July 1 assessment unless the new owner qualifies. Section 11-6B-3 covers owners 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled, who live there. Claims go to the county assessor by December 1.
